content: Lactucarium is a milky fluid secreted by various species of lettuce, particularly Lactuca virosa, and is typically extracted from the base of the plant's stems. It is often referred to as lettuce opium due to its sedative and pain-relieving properties. Lactucarium has been reported to induce a mild sense of euphoria. However, Lactuca virosa is toxic, and there has been at least one documented fatality associated with its misuse for intoxication purposes. As a latex, lactucarium physically resembles opium, as it is initially excreted as a white fluid that can be processed into a thick, solid form suitable for smoking. Historically, lactucarium, or lettuce opium, was utilized by the Ancient Egyptians and was introduced as a medicinal drug in the United States as early as 1799. During the 19th century, it was extensively studied and prescribed in Poland as a weaker but side-effect-free alternative to opium. In some cases, it was even considered preferable to opium. Despite these uses, early attempts to isolate an active alkaloid from lactucarium were unsuccessful. The substance was included in the 1898 United States Pharmacopoeia and the 1911 British Pharmaceutical Codex, where it was standardized for use in lozenges, tinctures, and syrups. It was primarily prescribed as a sedative for irritable coughs or as a mild hypnotic to treat insomnia. According to these codices, lactucarium was to be derived from Lactuca virosa, although smaller amounts could also be obtained from Lactuca sativa and Lactuca canadensis var. elongata. Interestingly, lactucarium from Lactuca scariola or Lactuca altissima was considered to be of superior quality. In the 20th century, two significant studies cast doubt on the efficacy of commercial lactucarium. In 1944, Fulton concluded that modern medicine regarded its sleep-inducing properties as mere superstition and its therapeutic effects as questionable or nonexistent. Another study identified active bitter compounds, including lactucin and lactucopicrin, in fresh latex. However, these compounds were found to be unstable and did not persist in commercial lactucarium preparations. As a result, the use of lactucarium declined. It experienced a brief resurgence in the mid-1970s when the hippie movement promoted it as a legal drug capable of inducing euphoria, often in combination with other substances like catnip or damiana. Additionally, lettuce seeds have historically been used for pain relief. In Avicenna's The Canon of Medicine, lettuce seed was ranked between belladonna and snow in terms of anesthetic potency. This text served as a key medical reference from the 11th to the 17th century. In contemporary times, lactucarium is no longer widely used as a pain reliever but remains available in some markets, often marketed as a legal psychotropic substance. In Iran, the seeds of common lettuce (Lactuca sativa) are still used in traditional medicine. A crude extract of these seeds has demonstrated analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects in standard laboratory tests on rats, without exhibiting toxicity at doses of up to 6 grams per kilogram. The active components of lactucarium are believed to include lactucin, lactucopicrin, and 11β13-dihydrolactucin. These compounds have been shown to possess analgesic effects comparable to or greater than those of ibuprofen in standard pain sensitivity tests, such as the hot-plate and tail-flick assays in laboratory mice. Additionally, lactucin and lactucopicrin have demonstrated sedative effects, as evidenced by reduced spontaneous movement in mice. Some of lactucarium's effects may also be attributed to trace amounts of hyoscyamine found in Lactuca virosa, although this alkaloid is not detectable in standard lactucarium preparations. Lactucarium was historically used in its unmodified form in lozenges, with doses ranging from 30 to 60 milligrams (0.5 to 1 grain), sometimes combined with borax. However, it was found to be more effective when formulated as a cough syrup, known as Syrupus Lactucarii (U.S.P.). This syrup contained 5% lactucarium, 22% glycerin, 5% alcohol, and 5% orange-flower water in a syrup base.
